launch.name: VS Code Workspace
launch.summary: Opens the multi-root workspace file in VS Code, full screen 1, with Fork beside it on screen 2.

launch.name: Fork
launch.summary: Opens Fork full screen 2, beside VS Code, for branches and diffs.

launch.name: Work Orca
launch.summary: Orca on the default profile (%APPDATA%\orca), full screen 1: the one Orca on this machine, holding the work repos that `devenv orca apply` registers and the estate repos (rig) that `rig estate orca --apply` registers. On a re-run `window_pid_file` picks the window owned by the pid Orca records in orca-runtime.json.

launch.name: Work Triage
launch.summary: The rig triage queue (`rig triage`) in an ordinary Chrome window on the work profile, full screen 2, beside Orca: starts the rig web dashboard if it is not already answering, then opens its triage inbox. The triage window also gives the rest of the dashboard. `--new-window` makes Chrome open a window even though the Admin desktop's work-profile window already exists, and `window_title` matches every dashboard page (`Rig / Triage`, `Rig / Estate`) as well as the title it loads with (`Rig // Estate Management`), so a later restore finds the window again.

launch.name: Google - Work Profile
launch.summary: Opens one Chrome window with the work profile, with Gmail, Google Meet and Calendar tabs, filling screen 1.

launch.name: Personal Warp
launch.summary: Single Warp session for personal-side work on screen 2, replacing the two Claude terminals. Each plain warp.exe launch opens a new window; `cwd` opens it in the personal workspace root (title 'pwsh in rig'). Warp can't auto-run a command on Windows, so run `claude` yourself.

launch.name: Personal Browser
launch.summary: Opens Chrome with the Profile 1 personal profile. Shares {chrome-user-data} with the Admin desktop's Profile 4 windows, so the launched PID hands off to the existing browser process and every Chrome window looks identical to `window_process_name` alone. `--new-window` forces a window to actually appear instead of focusing an existing Profile 1 one, and `window_title` pins the match to the personal Gmail window - without both, restore binds to whatever chrome.exe window shows up next and has previously grabbed work-profile windows.

launch.name: VS Code (rig)
launch.summary: Opens the rig repo folder in its own VS Code window. Deliberately opens the folder rather than rig.code-workspace: the IDE desktop owns that multi-root workspace file, and VS Code focuses the already-open workspace window instead of opening a second one, so two desktops opening the same .code-workspace collide onto one window. A plain folder window is a distinct VS Code window.

launch.name: Lab T3 Code
launch.summary: T3 Code under evaluation, full screen 1. Orca moved to the Work desktop, which owns both Orca profiles; a Lab entry would grab one of their windows. Install or upgrade it with `devenv tools` (winget `T3Tools.T3Code`).

launch.name: Lab Terminal
launch.summary: A plain Claude Code session beside T3 Code, for running the same task each way. Fork is not on this desktop: it keeps one window, which the first desktop already places.

background.name: Docker Desktop
background.summary: Starts at sign-in for the WSL engine and opens its Containers dashboard, which belongs in the tray. Closing the dashboard leaves the engine running. Turning off Open Docker Dashboard when Docker Desktop starts, in the Docker settings, stops the window at the source; this entry keeps it off the desktops either way.

notes: Bundle-style workspace plan that loads one file per desktop.
Bundle aliases are available anywhere placeholders are supported.
Desktop paths are resolved relative to this file.

Feature flags and their defaults live in the rig flags registry (`rig flags list`); `rig flags enable|disable NAME` stores a machine override in rig.db. Entries carry a `feature` name; a feature that is off disables its entries exactly as `disabled: true` would, so a variant can be paused without deleting its configuration.

A desktop ref can carry a `feature` too. A desktop behind a switched-off feature is not created at all and the desktops after it move up, so `personal-desktop: false` means three desktops, not four with an empty one.

Switching a desktop's feature off also retires it: restore removes a leftover virtual desktop past the planned count that carries that desktop's name, moving its windows to the last kept desktop. Other extra desktops are left alone. `--enable personal-desktop` brings it back.

`experimental-desktop` adds a trailing Lab desktop for evaluating new tooling (currently T3 Code) without disturbing the daily desktops. It is off by default; try it for one run with `workspace restore --enable experimental-desktop`.
`orca-sessions` puts Orca on the Work desktop's screen 1: one profile holding the work repos and rig. Screen 2 holds the rig triage inbox.
Desktop names (IDE, Work, Admin, Personal, Lab) are re-applied on every restore; `workspace name-desktops` re-applies them (and retires switched-off desktops) on demand.

Aliases here are defaults. `{localappdata}`, `{appdata}`, `{userprofile}` and `{programfiles}` come from the environment, and `tools.desktop.aliases` in `~/.workspace/config.json` overrides or adds any alias on one machine (`chrome-profile-work`, `workspace-root`, an app path).
Override a default for one run with `workspace restore --enable NAME` / `--disable NAME`. Inspect with `workspace features`.
